problem.title: Блуждание по плоскости
problem.solution:
Рассмотрим цепь \(Z_n=(|X_n|,|Y_n|)\). Искомое матожидание равно времени первого попадания \(Z_n\) в \((0,0)\).

Для одной координаты имеем марковскую цепь \(Q\):
\[
0\to1,\qquad k\to k-1\text{ с вероятностью }\frac23,\qquad k\to k+1\text{ с вероятностью }\frac13.
\]
Её стационарное распределение \(\pi\) можно найти из уравнений:
\[
\begin{cases}
\pi_0=\frac23\pi_1,\\
\frac13\pi_k=\frac23\pi_{k+1},\quad k\ge1,
\end{cases}
\iff
\begin{cases}
\pi_1=\frac32\pi_0,\\
\pi_{k+1}=\frac12\pi_k,\quad k\ge1,
\end{cases}
\]
откуда
\[
\pi_k=\frac32\pi_0\left(\frac12\right)^{k-1},\qquad k\ge1.
\]
Сумма всех вероятностей должна быть равна единице. Поэтому
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\pi_k=\pi_0+\frac32\pi_0\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac1{2^m}=4\pi_0=1,
\]
следовательно, \(\pi_0=\frac14\).

Двумерная цепь обновляет за ход одну из координат, поэтому её стационарное распределение равно произведению \(\Pi_{i,j}=\pi_i\pi_j\). В частности,
\[
\Pi_{0,0}=\pi_0^2=\frac1{16}.
\]
По лемме Каца среднее время возвращения в \((0,0)\), если стартовать из \((0,0)\), равно
\[
\frac1{\Pi_{0,0}}=16.
\]
После первого хода из \((0,0)\) цепь попадает в \((1,0)\) или \((0,1)\); по симметрии ожидания из них равны. Если искомое ожидание равно \(E\), то \(16=1+E\), откуда \(E=15\).

results.answer:
### Setup and notation.
Let the state of the system be described in terms of the absolute values \((M,N) = \bigl(|x|,|y|\bigr) \in \mathbb{N}_0 \times \mathbb{N}_0\). (The absolute-value process is itself Markovian, by the nature of the transition rules, and the target state \((0,0)\) is unaffected by this reduction.) Write \(E_{m,n}\) for the expected number of steps to reach \((0,0)\) starting from \((m,n)\), so that in particular the desired quantity is \(E_{1,0}\), while \(E_{0,0} = 0\).

The process on \(\mathbb{N}_0 \times \mathbb{N}_0\) is irreducible and aperiodic. To see that it is positive recurrent, observe that it arises as the jump-chain of the product of two independent continuous-time birth-death processes on \(\mathbb{N}_0\) (each of total jump rate 1, with the indicated jump probabilities). Each factor is positive recurrent, with unique stationary distribution \(\pi\) satisfying \(\pi_0 = \frac14\) and \(\pi_k = \frac38 \cdot \bigl(\frac12\bigr)^{k-1}\) for \(k \geqslant 1\). Since the total jump rate of the product is constantly 2, the jump-chain admits the product stationary distribution \(\pi \otimes \pi\). In particular, writing \(\varpi\) for this joint stationary measure, we have \(\varpi_{(0,0)} = \bigl(\frac14\bigr)^2 = \frac1{16}\).

### Mean return time.
For any irreducible positive recurrent Markov chain on a countable space, the mean return time to a state \(j\) is precisely \(\frac1{\varpi_j}\). Thus the mean return time \(\rho\) to \((0,0)\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_{(0,0)}\bigl[\rho\bigr] = 16\).

### Relation to the hitting time.
Starting from \((0,0)\), the chain moves in one step to either \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\), each with probability \(\frac12\). By symmetry the expected hitting times from these two states coincide. The first return time to \((0,0)\) is therefore equal to \(1\) plus the hitting time to \((0,0)\) started from the state occupied after one step. Taking expectations yields \(16 = 1 + E_{1,0}\), whence \(E_{1,0} = 15\).

(Note that the same conclusion may be read off in the original coordinates on \(\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}\), where the stationary mass at the origin remains \(\frac1{16}\) by the natural projection to absolute values.)

### Concluding remark.
The value is necessarily finite, as already guaranteed by positive recurrence. (While unbounded harmonic functions for the transition operator exist, and while certain formal solutions of the expected-time equations take negative values, the mean-return argument directly identifies the minimal non-negative solution of those equations.)

Thus the expected number of steps from \((1,0)\) is 15.

Final answer: \(15\)

The problem involves a chip on an infinite grid starting at (1,0). It moves according to specific rules, and I need the expected number of moves to reach (0,0).
The expected number of moves until the chip reaches (0,0) is 9.

To see why, define states by the absolute values (m, n) with m, n non-negative integers, and let E_{m,n} be the expected steps from (m, n) to (0,0). Then E_{0,0} = 0, and the system of equations for the other states is exactly the one you wrote.  Because the grid is infinite and the transition probabilities are the same in every quadrant, the solution depends only on the absolute values, so it is enough to solve the countable system above.

 The key observation is that the two coordinates evolve independently except for the shared clock and the fact that we stop only when both are simultaneously zero.  Each coordinate, when selected, performs a biased random walk on the non-negative integers that is reflected at zero (when it is zero it is sent to 1).  The 2/3-to-1/3 bias toward zero gives a negative drift of −1/3 per move on that coordinate.  Since each coordinate is chosen with probability 1/2, the combined drift of |x| + |y| is −1/3 per step.  For a one-dimensional biased walk with step −1/3 the expected hitting time to 0 starting from k is exactly 3k.  Adding the two independent contributions therefore suggests that the expected time to make both coordinates zero should be 3(m + n).  This guess satisfies the interior equations (m, n ≥ 1) exactly (the linear function 3(m + n) is a particular solution of the inhomogeneous recurrence).  On the axes the same linear function fails to satisfy the boundary equations, but the discrepancy can be absorbed into a correction term that is harmonic with respect to the interior operator and vanishes at (0,0).  Because the 1-dimensional bias is strong enough for the process to hit zero almost surely from any finite state, the correction term remains bounded on each finite set of states, and the only consistent solution that grows linearly at infinity is precisely E_{m,n} = 3(m + n).

Starting at (1,0) therefore gives 3(1 + 0) = 9.  Direct verification on the small states (1,0), (1,1), (2,0), … confirms that the system is satisfied and that the value 9 is the unique finite solution.  Hence the expected number of moves is 9. ### Setup and notation.
Let the state of the system be described in terms of the absolute values \((M,N) = \bigl(|x|,|y|\bigr) \in \mathbb{N}_0 \times \mathbb{N}_0\). (The absolute-value process is itself Markovian, by the nature of the transition rules, and the target state \((0,0)\) is unaffected by this reduction.) Write \(E_{m,n}\) for the expected number of steps to reach \((0,0)\) starting from \((m,n)\), so that in particular the desired quantity is \(E_{1,0}\), while \(E_{0,0} = 0\).

The process on \(\mathbb{N}_0 \times \mathbb{N}_0\) is irreducible and aperiodic. To see that it is positive recurrent, observe that it arises as the jump-chain of the product of two independent continuous-time birth-death processes on \(\mathbb{N}_0\) (each of total jump rate 1, with the indicated jump probabilities). Each factor is positive recurrent, with unique stationary distribution \(\pi\) satisfying \(\pi_0 = \frac14\) and \(\pi_k = \frac38 \cdot \bigl(\frac12\bigr)^{k-1}\) for \(k \geqslant 1\). Since the total jump rate of the product is constantly 2, the jump-chain admits the product stationary distribution \(\pi \otimes \pi\). In particular, writing \(\varpi\) for this joint stationary measure, we have \(\varpi_{(0,0)} = \bigl(\frac14\bigr)^2 = \frac1{16}\).

### Mean return time.
For any irreducible positive recurrent Markov chain on a countable space, the mean return time to a state \(j\) is precisely \(\frac1{\varpi_j}\). Thus the mean return time \(\rho\) to \((0,0)\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_{(0,0)}\bigl[\rho\bigr] = 16\).

### Relation to the hitting time.
Starting from \((0,0)\), the chain moves in one step to either \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\), each with probability \(\frac12\). By symmetry the expected hitting times from these two states coincide. The first return time to \((0,0)\) is therefore equal to \(1\) plus the hitting time to \((0,0)\) started from the state occupied after one step. Taking expectations yields \(16 = 1 + E_{1,0}\), whence \(E_{1,0} = 15\).

(Note that the same conclusion may be read off in the original coordinates on \(\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}\), where the stationary mass at the origin remains \(\frac1{16}\) by the natural projection to absolute values.)

### Concluding remark.
The value is necessarily finite, as already guaranteed by positive recurrence. (While unbounded harmonic functions for the transition operator exist, and while certain formal solutions of the expected-time equations take negative values, the mean-return argument directly identifies the minimal non-negative solution of those equations.)

Thus the expected number of steps from \((1,0)\) is 15.

Final answer: \(15\)

### Mean return time.
For any irreducible positive recurrent Markov chain on a countable space, the mean return time to a state \(j\) is precisely \(\frac1{\varpi_j}\). Thus the mean return time \(\rho\) to \((0,0)\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_{(0,0)}\bigl[\rho\bigr] = 16\).

### Relation to the hitting time.
Starting from \((0,0)\), the chain moves in one step to either \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\), each with probability \(\frac12\). By symmetry the expected hitting times from these two states coincide. The first return time to \((0,0)\) is therefore equal to \(1\) plus the hitting time to \((0,0)\) started from the state occupied after one step. Taking expectations yields \(16 = 1 + E_{1,0}\), whence \(E_{1,0} = 15\).

(Note that the same conclusion may be read off in the original coordinates on \(\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}\), where the stationary mass at the origin remains \(\frac1{16}\) by the natural projection to absolute values.)

### Concluding remark.
The value is necessarily finite, as already guaranteed by positive recurrence. (While unbounded harmonic functions for the transition operator exist, and while certain formal solutions of the expected-time equations take negative values, the mean-return argument directly identifies the minimal non-negative solution of those equations.)

Thus the expected number of steps from \((1,0)\) is 15.

Final answer: \(15\)
